chasis.desc: Heavy and it splinters, but anyone can build it.
Light, but it snaps in hard crashes. With the 3D printer: cheaper, in any shape and color you want.
Like PLA but it doesn't snap: handles hits and heat.
The propellers sit inside ducts: it can brush against things and people without cutting anyone. Slow but very stable.
For long flights and carrying heavy cameras.

motores.desc: Pulled from an old drone. Thrust = per motor, on 3S with a 5" propeller.
Tiny and fast, for 3" ducted propellers. Thrust = per motor, on 4S.
Efficient with a 7" propeller. Long flights with a heavy camera.

baterias.desc: Lots of energy, but it can't deliver as much current: 15 % less thrust.

controladoras.desc: An ESP32 with a motion sensor (MPU6050): it levels itself, but altitude is up to you.
With the barometer it knows its altitude: let go of Space and it holds there.
The flight controller of racing drones: responds faster and finer than the ESP32.
A serious flight controller with GPS: let go of the sticks and it brakes and holds still.
Runs your neural network on the drone: it can fly itself (with the AI Pilot).

camaras.desc: The 10-dollar camera: it records, but it looks like an old video.
The gimbal keeps the horizon level and aims at the subject's height.
The gimbal removes almost all the shake from the image.

extras.desc: Rings around the propellers: required when people are nearby.
The 10 sensors the AI uses to dodge obstacles.

software_ia.sabe: Takes a position around the subject and films steadily (from the front, the side, from above).
The same, but it can film in the forest or between columns without crashing.
Follows something that moves or orbits around it (matches, cars, weddings). For multi-camera shots.

escs.desc: The one that came with the recycled motors.
Bidirectional DShot: the flight controller filters each motor's vibration (sharper image).
More than enough current for any motor.

radios.desc: The ESP32's on-board antenna. Free, but short range: any farther and it's failsafe.
An ESP32 with a connector and a dipole antenna: a bit more range.
Today's standard: a fast, stable link.
Long range: goes through trees and buildings.

montajes.desc: All the motor vibration reaches the image.
Four little rubber dampers between the frame and the camera: the image shakes much less.
A flexible mount printed in TPU (needs the 3D printer).

herramientas.desc: Prints PLA/PETG frames (40 % cheaper, in any shape and color you want) and TPU mounts.
Goes between the battery and the drone the first time you plug it in: if there's a short, it cuts the power and nothing burns.
Measures continuity and voltage: on the workbench it flags bad wires BEFORE you connect the battery.
An arm with an electric screwdriver and torque control: it tightens every screw of a step at once, without stripping a single thread.
Reads your parts' manual and puts every wire on its pad (and every connector in its socket). Uses the same wire as doing it by hand.
A robotic station: it solders every missing joint with just the right temperature, flux and solder. They always come out good.

formas.stretch: Stretch X (longer than wide: stable going forward)
formas.marco: Framed (a ring joins the arm tips: takes hits)

soldadura.desc: The classic: plug it in and it heats to about 340 °C, no knob. It struggles with big pads (the battery on the ESC).
With a temperature knob and a stand. It recovers heat quickly: battery pads are no longer a problem.
Heats in seconds and barely loses temperature on big pads. The one drone shops use.
With the solder molten, press (X) and it sucks almost all of it in one go. To remove bridges, extra solder or desolder a wire.
Flux-cored. A small joint uses ~0.1 g; a battery joint, ~0.3 g.
Cleans the pad so the solder wets. Each drop (F) uses 0.25 ml.
Red, black and colors, 22-26 AWG. Each wire you place uses 10 cm (a motor is 3).
Braided copper: put the braid on the solder (hold M) and with the iron on top it soaks it up. Finer than the pump.
